transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-08
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (Cascade Head of ML), Renee Park (Cascade CTO), Michael Zhou (Infra), Sara Li (PM)

Summary: Intro discovery focused on per-token unit economics and host vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs for an internal summarization/alerting product. Customer emphasized strict cost cap for pilot and needs clarity on batching/caching levers to hit <50ms p95 for short requests and acceptable unit cost for long-document summarization.

Topics: pricing per token, batching behavior, KV/prefix cache hit rates, expected QPS profile, pilot budget, SOC2 and KMS questions, canary/fallback routing to cheaper models.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Kim from Redwood. Priya and Sam are with me. hows the audio?
00:06 Liam: Good here, thanks.
00:12 Jordan: Quick agenda — understand your workload shape (tokens per call, QPS), budget constraints for pilot, and what success looks like. Then Priya will walk through levers — batching, cache, dedicated sizing.
00:26 Renee: Sounds good. For context, Cascade's use case is nightly document summarization plus a realtime alerting assistant; most of the realtime calls are short (150-700 tokens) but the batch summarization is long form — 2k to 8k tokens. We'll likely start with a 3-month pilot and a hard budget of roughly $30k / month.
00:47 Priya: Okay that mix matters a lot — short chat-like requests are latency sensitive, long-doc summarization is token dense and benefits hugely from batching and quantization. For long docs we often recommend Dedicated or Private because you can pin quantized variants and tune batching aggressively.
01:02 Michael: If we start hosted, are there automatic fallbacks to cheaper models if capacity is high? We worry about latency spikes.
01:09 Jordan: Yes — smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants or different regions. But note fallbacks may change cost and quality; we'll surface that in SLAs.
01:20 Liam: Can you talk specifics on per-token pricing and how batching reduces our effective token cost? Give me a worked example.
01:25 Priya: Sure. Our public hosted list price is X per input token and Y per output token — let me not quote marketing numbers on the call, we'll put the spreadsheet in writing. But conceptually: if you have 2k-token requests processed in a burst, continuous batching consolidates multiple requests into a single kernel dispatch and amortizes kernel overhead. If your average batch size is 4 requests, you see 20–35% per-token savings versus single-request baseline.
01:50 Sara: Where does KV cache come in for long docs? We have repeated queries over similar document prefixes.
01:55 Priya: KV (prefix) caching is huge for retrieval-augmented flows. If 60% of token computation hits cache, you avoid recomputing attention for those tokens, which can drop inference time and cost by >40% for those flows. Hit rate depends on how similar your prompts are and session stickiness.
02:12 Liam: For the realtime assistant we need p95 < 150ms for 300-token prompts. Is that realistic on hosted?
02:18 Priya: For 300 token prompts p95 <150ms is tough on shared hosted at high concurrency, but achievable on Dedicated with tuned batching and reserved capacity. Hosted can get close at low to moderate scale but you'd see more variability.
02:33 Renee: Our pilot budget is tight — $30k/mo — how would that map to expected throughput? We expect 10k short realtime calls per day and 1,500 long-doc summarizations per week.
02:43 Priya: Quick back-of-envelope: short calls ~400 tokens incl response => ~4M tokens/day => ~120M tokens / month. Long docs average 4k tokens => 6M tokens/week => ~24M tokens / month. Total ~150M tokens / month. At hosted list rates that may be in the ballpark of $X–Yk/mo (we'll send numbers). With Dedicated you get better unit economics at committed throughput but require a monthly reservation.
03:10 Michael: How big a Dedicated pool would we need for our burstiness? We have sudden morning spikes 50 QPS for 3–4 minutes.
03:18 Priya: We size for tail SLOs. For 50 QPS burst with mixed short and long tokens you might need a small fleet of A100-equivalent instances with concurrent streams configured; our autoscaling supports burst capacity but there's a tradeoff — reserved capacity lowers unit cost but you pay for the reservation. We can simulate your histogram once you share RPS distribution.
03:36 Liam: Quantization — can we get comparable quality on 4-bit quantized variants for long docs? That would massively reduce cost.
03:42 Priya: Many customers use 4-bit quant for low-latency and cost. For summarization quality you should run an eval — quality delta varies by model and prompt. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profile per workload; for some open models delta is negligible.
03:58 Sara: What about encryption/KMS and audit logs? We need KMS integration and per-request audit for compliance.
04:05 Jordan: We support customer-managed keys and HSM/KMS integrations on Private/Dedicated. Hosted supports BYOK with some restrictions; full audit logs and longer retention are available on enterprise plans. We'll share a SOC 2 pack + network diagram.
04:20 Renee: If we do Private (VPC), what's the onboarding timeline? We have an internal compliance gate that takes 6 weeks.
04:27 Jordan: Private onboarding commonly 4–8 weeks depending on network reviews and certs. We can fast-track if you sign a pilot commitment.
04:34 Liam: Ok can we talk about a concrete pilot structure? We want to validate cost assumptions and latency at production-ish load with a clear stop/go decision after 6 weeks.
04:42 Jordan: Typical pilot: 6–8 weeks, start with a hosted sandbox to validate correctness and basic perf, then run a 48–72 hour dedicated benchmark at your target QPS for realistic unit-econ. We provide a unit-econ spreadsheet and run the benchmark together. Goal is to get a tight per-request cost and p95 latency curve.
04:58 Michael: Any caveats re batching that we should know — like does batching increase latency for single short requests?
05:05 Priya: Yes batching improves throughput but can add a small queuing delay. We support latency SLOs with continuous batching heuristics — aggressive batching for cheap background jobs, latency-first routing for realtime requests. You can set route-level policies so your alert assistant gets minimal batching.
05:21 Sara: We'd like to quantify cache hit assumptions — what are realistic numbers for RAG flows?
05:26 Priya: Typical RAG with session stickiness sees 40–70% KV hits depending on user behavior; higher for repeated QA on the same doc. For nightly summarization cache isn't as helpful unless you chunk and dedupe prefixes. We can show sample runs.
05:42 Liam: How do we reason about model variants? Could we do a cheap baseline model for first pass then fall back to a higher-quality model if confidence low?
05:50 Jordan: Yes, can do cascaded routing: cheap model for draft, high-quality for refinement or low-confidence cases. This reduces average token cost but increases complexity in orchestration; Redwood Console supports multi-model rollouts and traffic-splitting rules.
06:05 Renee: For the pilot we only have $30k/mo. If dedicated reservation costs more upfront, can we do a hybrid — hosted for realtime assistant and dedicated for nightly summarization?
06:13 Priya: Absolutely. Hybrid is common: keep latency-critical short calls on hosted with small reserved concurrency and offload bulk summarization to Dedicated or Private where you can tune quantization and batching for best unit cost. We'll show modeled scenarios.
06:26 Michael: What's the SLA for Dedicated vs Hosted?
06:30 Jordan: Dedicated comes with stronger uptime and latency SLOs in the contract; hosted has standard availability but less strict latency SLOs. We'll surface exact SLA language in the contract doc.
06:40 Sam: (note) capturing follow ups: send pricing, SOC2, network diagram, run benchmarks.
06:45 Liam: Great. A couple more quick technical Qs — how deterministic is token accounting when you batch? We need exact cost attribution for chargeback.
06:53 Priya: Token accounting is per-request; even with batching we bill per logical token consumed. Batching only affects serving efficiency, not how tokens are metered. We also expose token-level cost breakdown in the Console.
07:08 Sara: Any gotchas with 8k documents — do we need to chunk differently?
07:13 Priya: For >4k tokens we recommend chunking, streaming outputs, and possibly using model offload to handle KV. We'll share best-practice chunking guidelines.
07:21 Renee: If we sign pilot, what's the next step today?
07:24 Jordan: We'll email the pilot proposal and unit-econ spreadsheet. Priya will propose benchmark config. Can you confirm sample traffic by Thurs? (2027-11-11)
07:32 Liam: Yes we can try to send the histograms and a sample doc set by then.
07:36 Jordan: Cool. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule the benchmark.

(occasional cross talk, filler)
08:15 Priya: I'll also attach a simple calc for batch sizing — basically relates request arrival rate, desired latency budget, and batch window to expected batch size and savings.
08:28 Michael: One note — we have strict egress rules; if we go hosted we may need a dedicated peering or Private option.
08:35 Jordan: Noted — we'll include network / peering options.

Recap (final 2 minutes):
- Jordan: Send unit-econ spreadsheet, SOC2 and network diagram (Jordan).
- Priya: Prepare Dedicated perf estimate and benchmark plan (Priya).
- Michael: Share traffic histograms and sample docs (Michael).
- Customer goal: confirm pilot budget and decision criteria by 2027-11-12.

End of call.
